This sample shows how a substantial film review lives alongside a brief viewing record. It is a demonstration of the reading layout, not a review or a statement of the owner’s views.

## Beginning with a detail

A review can begin with a specific image, a sound, or a transition. The introduction gives that detail room before moving into a larger argument. The title of the film, its director, and its release year sit beside the text, keeping the reading column clear.

The writing can move between description and interpretation without asking the reader to navigate a series of cards. Paragraphs remain in one continuous column. Longer passages have the space they need; a short observation can stand on its own.

## Watching, then returning

A log records the encounter. An article is a place to return to it. These are different forms, so each has its own address and publication date. The connected log below demonstrates that relationship.

> A quotation can be set apart from the argument while remaining part of the same reading rhythm.

The sentence above is original demonstration copy, not a quotation from the film or another author. Replace it with a properly credited quotation when writing a real review.

## Notes for a closer reading

- Describe the moment before interpreting it.
- Identify the version or screening when it matters.
- Separate a first response from a later reconsideration.

These are examples of the kinds of notes a review might contain. The finished piece can be as short or as substantial as its subject needs.
